title: Numerical Methods for IVPs
summary: Most real ODEs have no formula for the solution. We then compute the solution step by step on a computer. All methods in this chapter solve an IVP y' = f(x,y), \qquad y(x_0) = y_0 . We choose a step size $h$ and compute approximations $y_n \approx y(x_n)$…

intro.x: Most real ODEs have no formula for the solution. We then compute the solution step by step on a computer. All methods in this chapter solve an IVP
We choose a step size $h$ and compute approximations $y_n \approx y(x_n)$ at $x_n = x_0 + nh$.

blocks.x: Follow the tangent line for one step. Simple, but not accurate. The error at one step is of order $h^2$ and the total error (global error) is of order $h$. Halving $h$ halves the error.
It averages the slope at the start and the predicted slope at the end. Global error is of order $h^2$: halving $h$ cuts the error by about 4.

\begin{aligned}
k_1 &= f(x_n, y_n), \\
k_2 &= f\big(x_n + \tfrac h2,\ y_n + \tfrac h2k_1\big), \\
k_3 &= f\big(x_n + \tfrac h2,\ y_n + \tfrac h2k_2\big), \\
k_4 &= f\big(x_n + h,\ y_n + h\,k_3\big), \\
y_{n+1} &= y_n + \tfrac{h}{6}\big(k_1 + 2k_2 + 2k_3 + k_4\big).
\end{aligned}
Global error is of order $h^4$: halving $h$ cuts the error by about 16. This is the standard choice for hand-written code.

blocks.name: Derivation
blocks.title: Where the three methods and their errors come from

blocks.x: Euler. Taylor expansion of the exact solution:
y(x_n + h) = y(x_n) + h\,y'(x_n) + \tfrac{h^2}{2}y''(\xi).

Since $y' = f(x,y)$, dropping the last term gives $y_{n+1} = y_n + hf(x_n,y_n)$. The dropped term is the local error, of order $h^2$. To cover an interval of length $b-a$ we take $N = (b-a)/h$ steps, so the errors add up to about $N\cdot O(h^2) = O(h)$. This is the global error.
Heun. Integrate $y' = f(x,y)$ from $x_n$ to $x_{n+1}$:
y(x_{n+1}) = y(x_n) + \int_{x_n}^{x_{n+1}}f\big(x,y(x)\big)\,\dd x .

Euler uses the left-end value of the integrand (rectangle rule). The trapezoid rule uses both ends: $\frac h2\big(f_n + f_{n+1}\big)$. The value $f_{n+1} = f(x_{n+1}, y_{n+1})$ needs the unknown $y_{n+1}$, so we predict it with an Euler step: $y^* = y_n + hk_1$. This gives $k_2 = f(x_{n+1}, y^*)$ and $y_{n+1} = y_n + \frac h2(k_1+k_2)$. The trapezoid rule has local error $O(h^3)$, so the global error is $O(h^2)$.
RK4. Use Simpson’s rule on the same integral:
\int_{x_n}^{x_{n+1}}f\,\dd x \approx \frac h6\big(f_n + 4f_{n+1/2} + f_{n+1}\big).

The midpoint slope $f_{n+1/2}$ is estimated twice ($k_2$ from an Euler half-step, $k_3$ from a corrected half-step), so $4f_{n+1/2}\approx 2k_2 + 2k_3$. The end slope $f_{n+1}$ is estimated by $k_4$. This gives $y_{n+1} = y_n + \frac h6(k_1 + 2k_2 + 2k_3 + k_4)$. Matching the Taylor series shows the local error is $O(h^5)$, so the global error is $O(h^4)$.
Take $y' = x + y$, $y(0)=1$, $h = 0.1$. The exact solution is $y = 2e^{x} - x - 1$, so $y(0.2) = 1.2428055$.
Two steps are enough to see a large difference: RK4 costs four function evaluations per step, but it is far more accurate.
Figure: Euler’s method with $h=0.2$ for $y'=x+y$. At $x=1$ it gives 2.977 and the exact value is 3.437. The error grows because each step follows the tangent line of a convex curve.

Smaller $h$ gives more accuracy but more work. There is also a stability limit. Take $y' = -\lambda y$ with $\lambda>0$ (the exact solution decays). Euler gives $y_{n+1} = (1 - h\lambda)\,y_n$. The numbers decay only if $|1 - h\lambda| < 1$, that is
h < \frac{2}{\lambda}.

For $y' = -10y$, step $h=0.3$ gives $y_{n+1} = -2y_n$. The numerical solution grows and flips sign, but the real solution decays. A system with very fast and very slow parts is called stiff. Stiff systems need very small steps with these methods, or special implicit methods.
The same formulas work for systems if $y$ and $f$ are vectors. For a second-order ODE, first convert it to a system (Chapter 3).
$y'' + y = 0$, $y(0)=1$, $y'(0)=0$. Let $u = y$ and $v = y'$. Then $u' = v$ and $v' = -u$. With $h=0.1$, one Euler step gives
(The exact solution is $y=\cos x$, and $\cos 0.1 = 0.995$.)

def rk4(f, x0, y0, h, n):
    x, y = x0, y0
    for _ in range(n):
        k1 = f(x, y)
        k2 = f(x + h/2, y + h/2*k1)
        k3 = f(x + h/2, y + h/2*k2)
        k4 = f(x + h,   y + h*k3)
        y += h/6*(k1 + 2*k2 + 2*k3 + k4)
        x += h
    return y

print(rk4(lambda x, y: x + y, 0, 1, 0.1, 2))   # about 1.242805
